turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil regarded Sandip with a measured gaze, his expression betraying neither agreement nor disagreement. He observed that Sandip’s inquiries were superfluous; the source of his apprehension was irrelevant to the matter at hand, and concerned him not. He then stated that the protection of his tenants would continue to be a priority, regardless of Sandip’s assessments.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip allowed a theatrical sigh to escape his lips, his gaze sweeping over the room with an exaggerated air of melancholy. He inquired of Nikhil, with a tone of feigned innocence, whether the landowner truly believed that his pronouncements on the welfare of tenants held any sway over those who toiled on his land, or if they were merely a performance for the benefit of an audience—perhaps, even, a certain observant lady nearby.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil regarded Sandip with a quiet intensity. He stated that such insinuations were unnecessary and demonstrated a fundamental misunderstanding of his purpose; his actions were not for display, but dictated by responsibility. He requested that Sandip cease these unproductive diversions and address the matter at hand.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip’s gaze lingered on Bimala, and he remarked to Nikhil that it was a curious thing, he observed, how easily one could mistake responsibility for mere theatricality. He suggested that one might even argue that the truest performances were often those that appeared most sincere, adding, perhaps, that this echoed the sentiments of Sophocles’ Antigone. He concluded with the thought that it was a tragic irony, he believed.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala regarded Sandip with a stillness that bordered on fragility, her fingers twisting unconsciously at the edge of her sari. She observed that the echoes of Sophocles seemed… distant, somehow, in this room, and that perhaps tragedy resided not only in defiance, but also in the quiet acceptance of obligations. Her gaze shifted briefly to Nikhil, then back to Sandip, a subtle question lingering in her eyes.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil observed that such literary allusions served only to obscure the present reality, and that dwelling on ancient tragedies would not alleviate the concerns at hand. He stated that if Sandip possessed information regarding genuine threats to his household or tenants, he should present it directly, rather than cloaking it in elaborate pronouncements. He requested Sandip to be forthright.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip allowed his gaze to rest upon Nikhil, a faint, almost imperceptible smile playing on his lips. He remarked that the landowner’s insistence on practicality was, of course, admirable—a virtue, one might say—but did it not also betray a certain… naivete? Surely, a man of Nikhil’s standing understood that the world rarely adhered to such straightforward narratives.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil regarded Sandip, his expression unchanged. He stated that the perception of naivete was a misjudgment, born, perhaps, of a failure to appreciate the complexities of managing a household and its surrounding lands. He requested that Sandip articulate the nature of these perceived 'straightforward narratives' he believed Nikhil to misunderstand.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip observed that it was amusing, truly, how readily a man might dismiss nuance, particularly when it concerned matters of consequence. He inquired, with a carefully cultivated air of disinterest, whether the landowner truly believed that the anxieties of his tenants, the whispers of discontent carried on the wind, could be so easily brushed aside with a curt dismissal of ‘straightforward narratives,’ as if the currents of human emotion flowed as predictably as irrigation channels.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala’s fingers tightened further on her sari, a slight tremor betraying the quiet tension in the room. She suggested, her voice barely audible, that perhaps the currents Sandip spoke of were not always borne of discontent, but sometimes, simply of a longing for understanding—a longing that could be misinterpreted, easily inflamed. She glanced at Nikhil, a silent plea for reassurance flickering in her eyes before returning her gaze to Sandip.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil regarded Sandip with a measured gaze, and stated that while he appreciated the observation regarding the currents of human emotion, he found it unproductive to speculate on their origins without concrete evidence of disruption. He requested that Sandip refrain from employing such rhetorical devices and instead focus on the information he claimed to possess.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip let out a theatrical sigh, his gaze drifting towards a portrait on the wall before returning to Nikhil. He remarked that it was remarkably convenient, this insistence on concrete evidence, especially when one considered the subtle shifts in the prevailing winds—the murmurings of those self-appointed moral arbiters who found such delight in condemning perceived deviations from the righteous path. Surely, even a man so grounded in the practicalities of land and ledger could perceive the danger lurking just beyond the confines of his meticulously managed estate?

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala observed the subtle tightening of Nikhil’s jaw, a fleeting display of contained tension. She inquired softly, more to the air than to either man, whether these 'moral arbiters' Sandip mentioned held such sway that even the quietest of doubts could be amplified into something… more substantial, something that might unsettle the peace of the region.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip allowed a wry smile to play upon his lips, his eyes lingering on Bimala before turning back to Nikhil. He suggested, with a tone of mock-sympathy, that perhaps the landowner's insistence on 'concrete evidence' was merely a symptom of a deeper, more unsettling blindness – a refusal to acknowledge the shadows that lengthen as the sun descends, and the potential for those shadows to conceal dangers far more insidious than any simple disruption.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala’s gaze drifted to the window, her fingers tracing the pattern of the embroidered fabric on her sleeve. She inquired of Sandip, her voice low and measured, whether his concern for the region’s peace truly stemmed from a desire for stability, or if it served a less discernible purpose.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip chuckled softly, his gaze flickering between Bimala and Nikhil, a theatrical gesture of amusement. He inquired, with a deliberate air of innocence, whether the lady’s astute question implied a suspicion of his motives, or merely reflected a commendable, albeit perhaps naive, desire for transparency—a quality, he mused, so rarely encountered in men of influence. It was, he suggested, a most flattering assessment, even if somewhat… misplaced.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala’s fingers stilled on the fabric, and she turned her head slightly, her eyes meeting Sandip's with an unreadable expression. She inquired, her voice barely a whisper, if a desire for transparency was truly so rare, or if perhaps some men simply preferred to operate under a veil of carefully constructed ambiguity.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip raised an eyebrow, allowing a languid sigh to escape his lips. He remarked, with a tone of affected weariness, that it appeared the lady possessed a rather… *romantic* view of ambiguity, as if obfuscation were an art form to be admired rather than a failing to be deplored – a curious sentiment, he observed, coming from one who presumably moved within circles of such perceived refinement. He directed his gaze towards Nikhil, a subtle challenge flickering within his eyes.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil regarded Sandip with a measured gaze, his expression betraying neither agreement nor disagreement. He stated that while he appreciated the observation regarding the perceived refinement of those in his circle, he found the digression unnecessary and, frankly, unproductive. He requested that Sandip return to the matter of the concerns regarding potential unrest among the Muslim population.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip allowed his gaze to linger on Nikhil for a moment longer, a theatrical sigh escaping his lips once more. He then remarked, with a carefully cultivated air of concern, that the landowner’s dismissal of his observations was a rather unfortunate display of… *prudence*, especially considering the precariousness of the situation – a prudence, he suggested, that could easily be mistaken for indifference, and indifference, as history so often demonstrates, can be a most fertile breeding ground for discontent. He directed his words primarily towards Nikhil, but his eyes flickered towards Bimala, ensuring she understood the implicit warning.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip inquired of Bimala as to where she intended to flee, addressing her as Queen.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip remarked to Nikhil that he questioned why Browning was not among his books, recalling a conversation with Bimala about a college contest involving Browning's translation, and asking if Nikhil remembered it.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip explained to Nikhil that he had managed to translate Browning into Bengali, though the result was far from a lasting joy for Bengal, and that he once believed himself on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence had intervened. He then recalled old Dakshina, suggesting that had he not become a Salt Inspector, he would have been a poet.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip informed Bimala that it was pointless for her to search the bookshelves, as Nikhil had ceased reading poetry since his marriage, and that he suspected a return of his poetic inspiration.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip stated that Nikhil had come to give him a warning.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip inquired of Nikhil whether the warning concerned his poetic inspiration.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that Mahomedan preachers had been stirring up the local Mussulmans, who were agitated and might attack him at any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had come to advise flight.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil clarified to Sandip that he had come to provide information, not to offer advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip commented to Nikhil that a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for him, had the estates been his, and suggested that Nikhil's weakness was also undermining neighboring zamindars.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil pointed out to Sandip that he had not offered advice, and requested that Sandip refrain from giving it, adding that it was futile. He then stated that he needed to inform Sandip that his followers had been secretly oppressing his tenantry, and demanded that he leave his territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip questioned Nikhil, asking whether the threat was due to fear of the Mussulmans or some other apprehension.
